statement: In a quiz, wrong answers lose no points. Each question has 5 choices and only one is right. Leo guesses all 20 questions at random. About how many should he expect to get right?

choices.misconception: I thought guessing never gets anything right, so it is not worth doing.
I divided 20 by 4, the number of wrong choices, instead of by 5, the number of choices.
I thought a guess is right half of the time, like tossing a coin.
I worked out how many he should expect to get wrong instead of right.

hints: How likely is a single random guess to be right?
One guess among 5 choices is right about 1 time in 5. Use that to share out the 20 questions, and compare with leaving them blank.
About 1 guess in every 5 is right. 20 questions are 4 groups of 5, so Leo should expect about 4 right answers, which is 4 more than if he left them blank.

solutions.reliable: With 5 choices, a random guess is right about 1 time in 5. Twenty questions make 4 groups of 5, so Leo should expect about 4 right. Leaving the questions blank would score nothing, and wrong answers cost nothing, so guessing can only help. The transferable idea: when wrong answers cost nothing, a guess is always worth more than a blank.

whyOnTest: When wrong answers lose nothing, a blank wastes points: random guessing earns about one right answer in every five, for free.
